entry.title: iPhone Duo screen cracks: what iFixit found
entry.summary: 2 minute read iPhone Duo screen cracks: what iFixit found 3:09 iFixit's teardown suggests the iPhone Duo's hinge center support bar may be behind its cracked inner screens. Apple is reportedly replacing affected phones. iFixit has torn down the iPhone Duo and given it a provision
entry.content:
2 minute read
iPhone Duo screen cracks: what iFixit found
3:09

iFixit's teardown suggests the iPhone Duo's hinge center support bar may be behind its cracked inner screens. Apple is reportedly replacing affected phones.

iFixit has torn down the iPhone Duo and given it a provisional 5/10 repairability score. That might not seem great, but it is the highest score it has awarded a foldable to date, which tells you a lot about the complexity of these devices. And it is partly that complexity that seems to be leading to multiple reports of cracked screens from around the world.

First off, let’s look at what iFixit found. The inner display has a matte nano-texture finish that scatters reflections in an attempt to hide the crease. With it removed, the crease looks arguably more visible than on, say, the Galaxy Z Fold8. Looking at the area under a microscope reveals that some subpixels are oval and point in different directions. iFixit points to an Apple patent application on reducing diffraction artifacts as a possible explanation.

 

 

The nano-texture finish sits on a replaceable polymer cover. Replacing it costs $49 ($19 with AppleCare+) at an Apple Store, while replacing the inner display costs $999 without coverage, half the price of a new device.

The hinge itself uses metal joints, springs, and synchronization gears around a teardrop-shaped curve, so the closed screen follows a gentle curve inside the hinge. If that sounds simple, it’s actually not, as the display’s layers also need to slide against each other while it curves round.

Cracking on

So, what’s causing the cracks? To find out, iFixit built a 3D model of the hinge based on a combination of teardown footage, patents, and CT scans. It then compared this with the reported damage locations, which mostly follow the same pattern: a thin line along the fold and a brighter, thicker line extending horizontally across the right-hand side of the screen just below the halfway point. Users also report hearing a loud pop just before the screen breaks.

iFixit’s model places the breaks slightly below the cable’s path through the hinge, and its simulation shows that the center support bar can fail to drop far enough to accommodate the folded screen. This would create a stress hotspot near where the breaks have been reported.

It’s worth pointing out at the moment that this is a hypothesis, but iFixit’s testing and stellar track record in this area show that it’s a reasonable one. The question is, what happens next? Is this a small manufacturing defect affecting a tiny sample of new iPhone Duos, or a larger problem that will eventually affect most units? Given the extensive testing that the Duo went through you have to hope the former, but we’ve already seen some high-profile devices such as the Sony FX5 hit problems that you think would have been caught before release, so you never know.

Apple has yet to officially respond to what online wags are calling Crackgate, but so far reports are that Apple is replacing affected devices wholesale rather than trying to implement repairs.

entry.title: CIPA August 2026: camera and lens shipments
entry.summary: 2 minute read CIPA August 2026: camera and lens shipments 3:10 CIPA data shows camera makers shipped 3.2% fewer cameras from January to August, but shipped value rose 3.7% as prices rise. Full-frame fell almost 20% while compacts grew 15%. Japanese camera industry trade body CIPA
entry.content:
2 minute read
CIPA August 2026: camera and lens shipments
3:10

CIPA data shows camera makers shipped 3.2% fewer cameras from January to August, but shipped value rose 3.7% as prices rise. Full-frame fell almost 20% while compacts grew 15%.

Japanese camera industry trade body CIPA’s (Camera & Imaging Products Association) latest data has just been published, and the news from August 2026 is decidedly mixed. On the one hand, between January and August this year, member companies shipped 5.7 million digital cameras worldwide, 3.2% fewer than in the same period of 2025. On the other, the shipped value of all those cameras rose 3.7% to about ¥572 billion ($3.65 billion).

A weakness in the market for interchangeable-lens cameras (ILCs) accounts for the drop. Shipments of 4.01 million bodies were 9.3% down, yet their value rose 1.5% to about ¥465 billion ($2.97 billion). Mirrorless cameras, which make up 92% of ILC units, fell 6.2% to 3.7 million while value rose 3.4%.

By our calculations, that works out at roughly ¥122,000 ($778) shipped value per mirrorless body, about 10% more than a year ago.

Wider rumors of a resurgence in DSLRs seem wide of the mark, however. These fell 35% in terms of units and 37% in terms of value, and now make up under 8% of ILC shipments. Effectively, they’re a niche product nowadays.

There is a definite division along the lines of ILC sensor size. Cameras with 35mm or larger sensors fell 19.8% in units and 6.5% in value, while smaller-sensor models dipped 3.2% in units and gained 14% in value.

So, where is the growth coming from? Fixed-lens cameras basically, up 15.3% to 1.69 million units and 14.1% in value, which reached about ¥107 billion ($0.68 billion). They now make up almost 30% of everything CIPA members ship, and in August alone they were up almost a third on the year.

It’s worth pointing out that lenses are still holding up better compared to bodies. Shipments of 6.31 million lenses were 4.9% lower, but value rose 4.4% to about ¥340 billion ($2.17 billion), and the lens-to-body ratio stands at 1.57, up from 1.50 a year ago, i.e. 1.57 lenses are shipped for every camera body.

Regionally, China (down 20.8%), the Americas (down 12.9%), and Europe (down 10.9%) were shipped fewer ILCs, while Asia outside Japan and China rose 12.3%, and Japan 6.7%.

CIPA’s February forecast of 6.82 million ILC bodies for the year now looks out of reach, as it would require monthly shipments about 40% above the year-to-date average. The comparison also flatters the 2026 figures, because CIPA added Kenko Tokina to its camera statistics from January and has not adjusted year-on-year figures. That means any like-for-like declines are probably steeper than reported.

entry.title: Adobe BWT Alpine F1 partnership: AI fan experience
entry.summary: 2 minute read Adobe BWT Alpine F1 partnership: AI fan experience 2:34 Adobe will become BWT Alpine Formula One Team's Official AI Fan Experience Partner next season in a deal that covers content creation, fan data, AI search visibility, and design tools. We’ve already written abo
entry.content:
2 minute read
Adobe BWT Alpine F1 partnership: AI fan experience
2:34

Adobe will become BWT Alpine Formula One Team's Official AI Fan Experience Partner next season in a deal that covers content creation, fan data, AI search visibility, and design tools.

We’ve already written about F1 once this week. Now comes a second chance for us to blather on about bargeboards and tire strategies as Adobe and the BWT Alpine Formula One Team have announced a global premium partnership.

So far, this is less about Adobe Creative Cloud products being used in the Alpine marketing efforts, and more about Adobe becoming the Official AI Fan Experience Partner for the team. It’s going to be a bigger deal than it first appears, though. The partnership applies from the 2027 Formula One season and beyond, and next season the team’s main title sponsor becomes Gucci. That means the team name changes to the Gucci Racing Alpine Formula One Team, and you can expect its profile to start ramping up from there.

The partnership to date covers four initiatives. Adobe GenStudio, an AI-powered content production tool, will be used to create personalized content variations for fans. Adobe Experience Platform will give the team a real-time view of fan engagement, used to choose messages and channels, while Adobe Brand Visibility, an AI search optimization system, will show how the team appears across AI agents and LLMs. And finally Adobe Express will let the team offer fans design tools with generative AI image generation.

If all that covers a whole load of tools you are unfamiliar with, then likewise. But it does give an insight into how AI is inveigling its way into all areas of a major branding effort like those you associate with F1 teams. We’re sure it won’t be too long before we can start talking about things we’re more familiar with when it comes to the team’s activities.

And, as its 2027 driver line up announcement shows, Alpine has definitely got game.

The team is firmly in the midpack when it comes to F1. But even if it hasn’t made the jump up to the Big Four of Mercedes, Ferrari, McLaren, and Red Bull as yet this season, despite some promising results for French driver Pierre Gasly, leveling up its off-track activities is an important part of the F1 marketing mix. And the new Gucci branding is going to take it stratospheric.

Those that somewhat despair of encroaching ‘sleb culture on the grid might want to look away now. Which is funnily enough just what the TV director tends to do, normally when something interesting is going on on the racetrack, because there’s a Kardashian in the Ferrari garage. But we tend to get grumpy about such things and we digress…

entry.title: GoPro Mission 1 close-up filters: price, specs
entry.summary: 1 minute read GoPro Mission 1 close-up filters: price, specs 2:32 GoPro and PolarPro's Mission 1 diopters cost $49.99 for one or $99.99 for a set. The +2 cuts minimum focus to 30 cm (11.8 in). GoPro has officially announced three new close-focus diopters, made by PolarPro from op
entry.content:
1 minute read
GoPro Mission 1 close-up filters: price, specs
2:32

GoPro and PolarPro's Mission 1 diopters cost $49.99 for one or $99.99 for a set. The +2 cuts minimum focus to 30 cm (11.8 in).

GoPro has officially announced three new close-focus diopters, made by PolarPro from optical-grade multi-coated glass, for the Mission 1 series.

They were first flagged at the Mission 1 launch in May and address one of the range’s key weaknesses. While the new larger 1-in sensor in the cameras was welcomed by many, for a few users the fact that the close-focus distance suddenly increased to 60 cm (24 in) was a problem.

The new transparent filters slide over the camera lens or ND filter and use static focus, so no adjustment is required. A standalone +0.5 Close-Up Filter is pitched at vlog-style content, lifestyle footage, and travel shots, while a three-filter Close-Up Filter Set (+0.5, +1, and +2) is also available for more flexibility. As is usually the case with these filters, increasing diopter strength increases subject separation and gives a shallower depth of field.

Distance details

Focus distances are 50 cm (19.7 in) to 150 cm (59 in) for the standalone +0.5 filter, 45 cm (17.7 in) to 90 cm (35.4 in) for the +1, and 30 cm (11.8 in) to 50 cm (19.7 in) for the +2. For uses such as shooting in confined spaces like car interiors, where the 60 cm limit was a problem, the stronger filters bring subjects within reach, although each strength also caps how far away you can focus.

Users have to stack the diopters in front of ND filters rather than the other way around, though GoPro says that camera tracking in VLOG mode does not track subjects well when an ND filter and a diopter are stacked. It also notes that the far focus on the +0.5 is limited to 150 cm to create the subject separation and depth-of-field effect, and high-vibration activities and quick camera movements may affect video stabilization with the +2.

Pricing and availability

The standalone Close-Up Filter costs $49.99, while the Close-Up Filter Set costs $99.99. Both are available now globally at GoPro.com. They are compatible with the Mission 1 and Mission 1 PRO, as well as the Mission 1 PRO Grip Edition, Creator Edition, and Ultimate Creator Edition, and are backed by PolarPro’s Adventure Assurance.

entry.title: Sigma FP2: price, specs, and release date
entry.summary: 3 minute read Sigma FP2: price, specs, and release date 4:49 The Sigma FP2 costs $2199 body-only and arrives November 11. It has a 24.5-megapixel sensor, records 6K OpenGate, but the internal EVF rumors were wide of the mark. Sigma’s much-anticipated FP2 L-Mount full-frame camera
entry.content:
3 minute read
Sigma FP2: price, specs, and release date
4:49

The Sigma FP2 costs $2199 body-only and arrives November 11. It has a 24.5-megapixel sensor, records 6K OpenGate, but the internal EVF rumors were wide of the mark.

Sigma’s much-anticipated FP2 L-Mount full-frame camera has been officially unveiled. It will be available on Wednesday, November 11, 2026 at authorized Sigma retailers starting at $2199 (body only). It will also be sold as a bundle with the 50mm F2 DG | Contemporary lens ($2749) or the Electronic Viewfinder EVF-21 ($2749).

That gives you a steer on the biggest rumor involving the camera not coming to pass. Back in early October, numerous sources (including us, mea culpa) stated confidently that the FP2 would integrate an EVF into the camera body. That hasn’t happened. On the plus side, neither has the rumored $2500 price point. Swings and roundabouts and all that.

Sigma claims the FP2 has the world’s smallest full-frame body and it certainly is small. It comes in at a meager 112.8 x 69.9 x 41.8 mm (4.4 x 2.8 x 1.6 in) and weighs 446 g (15.7 oz) including battery. Body only is an even more impressive 388 g (13.7 oz).

It packs plenty into that, however. The camera has a 24.5-megapixel partially stacked CMOS sensor with high-speed readout that reduces rolling shutter distortion. It shoots continuously at up to approximately 20 fps for up to 200 frames in a single burst. Subject detection recognizes people, animals, and birds, while thirteen color modes are selectable with a dedicated “Color” button.

Sigma's pitching this as a proper hybrid, one that strips down to a pocketable street camera or builds up into a full production rig with cine lenses, matte boxes, and wireless monitors.

Video-first

Speculation pre-release pegged the downgrading of the sensor (the fp L offered 61 MP) as signposting a tilt toward video, and a video-heavy feature set bears that out, though the lack of IBIS could be an issue.

A dedicated switch on top of the body toggles between STILL and CINE modes, each with its own functions, user interface, and workflow. In CINE mode, the FP2 offers 6K OpenGate recording and up to 14.1 stops of dynamic range (4K FF L-Log), with 7 stops of highlight headroom at ISO 1250 and above. It has 70 GB of internal storage in addition to an SD card slot, with recording continuing to internal storage when the memory card is full. The card could fill fairly quickly, since the camera supports ProRes RAW. It also supports L-Log from Leica Camera AG and 32-bit float audio (though that requires the optional HU-21 hot shoe unit with the Panasonic DMW-XLR2 and DMW-DMS1).

The Director’s Viewfinder function simulates the shooting ranges of various brands’ cinema cameras, including the ARRI ALEXA 35 and Sony VENICE 2 / BURANO. A desqueeze display mode is available for anamorphic lenses, while the optional LCD Viewfinder LVF-21 (sold separately) lets users check the view on the optical axis. This mounts over the LCD monitor, cuts out extraneous light, has diopter adjustment from −2 to +1 dpt, and magnifies the LCD 2.5x.

The tilting rear LCD tilts up 90° and down 45°. As to the additional EVF accessory, the EVF-21 attaches via a single USB-C port and tilts upward by up to 90°. Designed specifically for the FP2, it comes with a large eye cup, and features a 0.5-inch OLED panel with approximately 5.76 million dots. We don’t have figures for its weight, but the photo below shows just how much extra area it takes up on the side of the camera.

Stills-wise, native ISO runs 100 to 102,400 and expands down to ISO 6 for stills. The shutter runs 30 seconds to 1/25,600, plus bulb up to five minutes, with flash sync at 1/50s without a crop. Sigma says battery life is approximately 30% longer than the original fp, providing enough juice for approximately 370 still images or about 130 minutes of video.

Pricing and availability

We've covered this already, but for those that skip to the end to find this information, the FP2  will be available on November 11 starting at $2199 (body only). It will also be sold as a bundle with the (equally new) 50mm F2 DG | Contemporary lens at $274, or the Electronic Viewfinder EVF-21, which is also $2749.

entry.summary: 3 minute read OPPO Find X10 Pro Max: specs, price, and cameras 5:31 The new OPPO Find X10 raises the bar for smartphone photography to an impressive level with up to three 200 MP rear-facing cameras, 17 stops, Open Gate, and a screen with 3600 nits peak brightness. Another week,
entry.content:
3 minute read
OPPO Find X10 Pro Max: specs, price, and cameras
5:31

The new OPPO Find X10 raises the bar for smartphone photography to an impressive level with up to three 200 MP rear-facing cameras, 17 stops, Open Gate, and a screen with 3600 nits peak brightness.

Another week, another top-flight camera phone from China, but even by the Chinese phone manufacturers’ recent hyperbolic standards, the OPPO Find X10 series, and the Find X10 Pro Max in particular, are something else.

Unlike some recent cracking phones from China, the Find X10 and Find X10 Pro Max will be available globally through official OPPO stores, with some markets already on sale. OnePlus has stopped launching new phones in North America and Europe, and the excellent OnePlus 16 is China-only, but OPPO is more than ready to fill the gap.

It’s also worth pointing out that they won’t be cheap. The cameras in these phones were co-developed with Hasselblad and, as the old beer commercial put it, are reassuringly expensive. Expect to pay north of $1000 for the Find X10 and not far off $2000 for the Pro Max. Yes, you can get an iPhone Duo for that.

But third, the Find X10 Pro Max is, according to OPPO, the first phone to feature three 200 MP rear cameras. And no, the iPhone Duo does not have those.

Camera details

The Find X10 has dual 200 MP rear cameras, and the Find X10 Pro Max has three. On the Pro Max, the ultra-wide uses a 1/1.56-inch sensor that captures twice as much light as the previous-generation models, paired with a 124° autofocus lens. The main camera uses the new 1/1.28-inch ISOCELL HPC sensor, developed with Samsung, and DeepPix technology gives it up to 17 stops of dynamic range.

The Pro Max telephoto has an f/2.1 aperture and a 10 cm (3.9 in) minimum focusing distance, and doubles as a telemacro camera. Default capture is 26 MP from ultra-wide through 9.9x, while Hasselblad Hi-Res Mode captures 50 MP or 200 MP on supported cameras. The OPPO Hasselblad Teleconverter gives 3.28x optical magnification on the 200 MP telephoto of both phones.

LUMO True Image Engine debuts alongside a New-Generation True Color Camera that captures multispectral color data. The engine brings the tonal approach of Hasselblad Master Mode into the default Photo mode and reduces sharpening, noise reduction, and AI-generated detail.

The Find X10 records 4K60 on all rear cameras, with 4K120 and 8K30 on its 200 MP main and telephoto cameras. The Pro Max goes further: all three 200 MP cameras support 4K60, 4K120, and 8K30.

And the spec-blitz keeps coming. Both phones support Dolby Vision, ACES-certified O-Log2, and Open Gate Capture, a first for an OPPO smartphone. Open Gate uses the full sensor area so footage can be cropped and reframed for different aspect ratios in post.

Dolby Vision, O-Log2, and Open Gate are also coming to Blackmagic Camera, with the optimized version scheduled for November. The Tilta Khronos Creator Kit for the Pro Max includes an additional handle, a 67mm filter adapter, an adapter for the Teleconverter, and an active cooling fan.

Phone-specific details

Both phones use One-Piece Sculpted Glass and have IP66, IP68, and IP69 ratings, plus SGS Five-Star Drop Resistance Certification. The Find X10 comes in Glacier Blue, Glow Coral, and Mist Grey. The Find X10 Pro Max comes in Titanium Grey and Luna White, which has a silver LUMO Camera Island and a matte orange accent ring on the camera module.

The displays measure 6.59 inches (Find X10) and 6.78 inches (Pro Max), with up to 144 Hz LTPO, Dolby Vision, dimming to 1 nit, and 3840 Hz PWM dimming. OPPO claims 3600 nits peak brightness. Both also support the BT.2020 color gamut, which OPPO says covers around 40% more color space than DCI-P3.

Both phones have an OPPO Silicon-Carbon Battery of up to 8000 mAh (7150 mAh in certain markets), 80 W SUPERVOOC wired charging, and 50 W AIRVOOC wireless charging. The Find X10 uses the 3 nm MediaTek Dimensity 9600M chip, and the Find X10 Pro Max uses the 2 nm Dimensity 9600 Pro. Both have vapor chamber cooling.

Both phones also run the new ColorOS 17. OPPO Lab data puts app launch stability up 55% on ColorOS 16, and says over 25% more apps can stay running in the background. AI Mind Pilot with Agent Mode, built with Manus, works with photos and files on the device across multiple steps. AI Photo Agent offers scene-based edit suggestions, natural-language edits, and Style Match from a reference image. AI Photo Agent is rolling out gradually, has monthly usage limits, and supports static images only.

Pricing and availability

Prices start at €1199 for the Find X10 and €1699 for the Find X10 Pro Max in markets where the phones are on sale, around $1340 and $1900 at current exchange rates. OPPO does not sell phones in the US, so buyers there will need an importer.

entry.summary: 2 minute read Insta360 Mic: price, specs, and availability 5:02 The new Insta360 Mic sits between the Mic Pro and Mic Air. Expandable storage allows optional 32-bit float internal recording, it features the Mic Pro's customizable E-Ink display, and prices start at $79.99. Insta36
entry.content:
2 minute read
Insta360 Mic: price, specs, and availability
5:02


The new Insta360 Mic sits between the Mic Pro and Mic Air. Expandable storage allows optional 32-bit float internal recording, it features the Mic Pro's customizable E-Ink display, and prices start at $79.99.

Insta360 has launched Insta360 Mic, a wireless microphone aimed at content creators. It sits neatly between the flagship Mic Pro and the entry-level Mic Air in the company’s lineup, and is Insta360’s first customizable E-Ink wireless mic with expandable storage. As with the Mic Pro, the transmitter’s E-Ink display shows images users upload, but this time around a microSD slot allows users access to more than the Mac Pro’s included 32 GB. Without a card, Mic records over Bluetooth or through the receiver.

With a microSD card inserted, the transmitter records 32-bit float audio internally, acting as a reliable backup to whatever is recorded on the accompanying camera or phone. AI noise canceling runs on a dedicated AI audio processing chip using an NPU-based noise reduction model. Two automatic gain modes are available to handle audio processing on the fly: Auto, which helps prevent clipping, and Dynamic, which balances volume changes. Three voice tone presets, Regular, Rich, and Bright, are also included.

One receiver connects up to four transmitters, and Mic and Mic Pro transmitters can be mixed on the same receiver. For multicamera work, two transmitters can send synchronized audio to up to four receivers. Each transmitter runs for up to 13 hours, extending to 34 hours with the charging case.

Connectivity and size

Insta360 Direct Connect pairs the transmitter over Bluetooth with the company’s own cameras, namely the X6, X5, Luna Ultra, Luna Pro, GO Ultra, and Ace Pro 2, recording 48 kHz audio without a receiver. The X6 and Luna can connect two transmitters at once. The receiver connects to smartphones, DSLRs, and mirrorless cameras through the included USB-C smartphone adapter or 3.5 mm cable. Clipped to a shirt or jacket, the transmitter works as a wireless lavalier microphone, with no cable running between the speaker and the camera.

Transmitter dimensions are 38×12.2mm (1.5×0.5in) and it weighs 19.4 g (0.7 oz). It uses the same receiver and charging case as the Mic Pro. These are 55.8×27.7×21mm (2.2×1.1×0.8in) and 29.8g (1.1oz), and 122×61.9×42.2mm (4.8×2.4×1.7in) and 174 g (6.1 oz) respectively.

Pricing and availability

Insta360 Mic launches globally on October 22, 2026, from the Insta360 Official Store, Amazon, and authorized retailers. Pricing is $249 for 2 transmitters + 1 receiver, $139 for 1 transmitter + 1 receiver, and $79.99 for a single transmitter.

entry.title: Leica Q3 43 Formula 1 Edition: price and specs
entry.summary: 2 minute read Leica Q3 43 Formula 1 Edition: price and specs 3:31 Leica's special edition F1 camera adds carbon fiber, a Microvelour body, and a wireless charging grip to the Q3 43, not to mention $2000. The Formula One circus heads to North America this weekend, with the US Gran
entry.content:
2 minute read
Leica Q3 43 Formula 1 Edition: price and specs
3:31

Leica's special edition F1 camera adds carbon fiber, a Microvelour body, and a wireless charging grip to the Q3 43, not to mention $2000.

The Formula One circus heads to North America this weekend, with the US Grand Prix at the fabulous Circuit of the Americas in Austin, Texas, kicking off the last six races of the year. And it has a new Leica camera edition in tow.

F1 has been owned by Liberty Media for several years now, and where the Americas-based races were once almost exercises in box-ticking, the combination of US ownership and the popularity juggernaut of Drive to Survive has seen them rise significantly in importance. Never mind that 20-year-old prodigy Kimi Antonelli can win the Drivers’ Championship five races early, and become its youngest champion ever, if he wins on Sunday and other results go his way, F1 in North America is now about serious marketing razzamatazz.

Now with added carbon fiber

Which brings us to the Leica Q3 43 Formula 1 Edition camera, a special edition of the Leica Q3 43, sold as a camera and accessories set. It has handcrafted carbon fiber parts, black Microvelour covering, official F1 branding, and naturally costs a small fortune.

The carbon fiber parts, specially manufactured in Germany, are fitted to the hand grip, thumb rest, and soft-release button. The soft-release button and the right-hand function button in the thumb rest are finished in Formula 1 red. The top plate is engraved with the F1 logo, the lens cap matches, and the rope strap bears both brands’ logos.

Thankfully, the godawful specially designed Formula1 font family that F1 uses in its broadcasts hasn’t made it anywhere near it.

The wireless charging hand grip is carbon fiber instead of the classic leatherette covering. It has an Arca-Swiss mount, can be removed at any time, and accepts a wrist strap. The camera starts charging when placed on the Drop XL Wireless Charger pad.

Leica Q3 43 base

Elsewhere, it is a bog-standard Leica Q3 43, if any camera of this pedigree can really be referred to as ‘bog-standard’. That gives you a 60 MP CMOS full-frame sensor, with a choice of 60, 36, or 18 MP in JPEG or DNG, any of which always use the entire sensor area. The ISO range is 50 to 100,000. Processing is handled by the Maestro IV processor with L² technology, and video recording goes up to 8K.

The lens is the Leica APO-Summicron 43 f/2 ASPH., which has seven aspherical surfaces and a built-in macro mode. The focus range is 60 cm (23.6 in) to infinity, with a macro setting of 26.5 cm (10.4 in) to 60 cm (23.6 in). Autofocus is a hybrid system combining contrast measurement, depth mapping, and phase detection, and the aperture runs from f/2 to f/16 in 1/3 EV increments. Dimensions are 130 x 80.3 x 97.6 mm (5.1 x 3.2 x 3.8 in).

One further differentiator, though, is a ‘Formula 1’ Leica Look developed specially for the camera. Leica says this applies greater contrast and saturation to still images, and can be transferred to the camera via the Leica FOTOS app.

Pricing and availability

The Leica Q3 43 Formula 1 Edition is available now for $9950, an impressive $2000 more than the base Leica Q3 43 currently is, but then this is Formula One.

OM System PEN delay: Japan release moves to Nov
2:21

OM System PEN release in Japan moves to November 28 after pre-orders exceeded expectations. Retailers elsewhere are still taking orders.

The Sony FX5 looks increasingly likely to meet its latest November 16 release date, nearly three months after it was originally meant to ship. But the supply problems affecting the camera industry continue with the OM System PEN the latest camera to slip down the schedules, at least in its Japanese home market.

In a machine-translated statement, OM Digital Solutions says it has postponed the release of the eagerly anticipated mirrorless camera and related accessories from October 30, 2026, to November 28, 2026.

The company says pre-orders exceeded expectations, and that only some customers could have received the product on release day, depending on type and color. It now plans to release the camera once it has secured enough stock for all customers who had confirmed pre-orders by September 10, the date of the first delivery delay notice.

The delay covers the PEN body (silver or black), the PEN 14-42mm F3.5-5.6 III lens kit (body plus M.ZUIKO DIGITAL 14-42mm F3.5-5.6 III), the PEN double zoom kit (body plus that lens and the M.ZUIKO DIGITAL ED 40-150mm F4.0-5.6 R), the BLS-7 battery, and the BCS-7 charger. The M.ZUIKO DIGITAL 14-42mm F3.5-5.6 III lens still goes on sale October 30 as planned.

As far as we can tell at the moment, this is a problem in Japan only. Retailers around the world are still listing the camera as either in stock or available for pre-order. PetaPixel’s fancy new Pixel Meter review aggregator gives it an 86/100 score, though, so it would not be impossible for demand to put stock under pressure elsewhere as well.

In related news, the entry deadline for the “My Journey, Written with PEN: OM SYSTEM PEN Launch Commemoration Campaign” moves from November 19, 2026, to April 19, 2027. The eligible purchase period (September 9 to November 5, 2026) is unchanged, and pre-orders or orders in that window qualify even if delivery comes later.

Cooke S4 FF/i: full-frame primes, specs and price
1:57

Cooke's S4 FF/i full-frame primes cover 18 to 100mm at T2.0. Close focus averages 385 mm (just over 15 in) and the set is available to order now.

Cooke has expanded its PL/LPL lens range with the S4 FF/i spherical primes, a full-frame evolution of its S4/i Super 35 lenses.

The set comprises six T2.0 primes: 18, 25, 35, 50, 75, and 100mm. It is a new lens design that retains some optical qualities of the original S4/i S35 but updated for full-frame cameras. Cooke says the range has a “class-leading close focus and a carefully regulated character that complements skin tones, delivers gentle clarity and expressive lens flares.”  Each focal length flares a little differently.

Bokeh is described as smooth and extremely circular wide open with gently defined edges. Toward the edges of the frame, it takes on a cat’s eye shape, and that change is consistent across the focal length range. A nine-blade iris with curved blades, in place of the S4/i S35’s eight straight blades, keeps bokeh rounder as you stop down.

Close focus averages what looks to be a class-leading 385 mm (just over 15 in). The lenses have also been designed very much with handling in mind. They average 1642 g (3.6 lb), 29% lighter than the original S4/i S35, and individual lenses weigh between 1.45 kg and 1.8 kg (3.2 lb and 4 lb) including the PL mount. Front diameter is 87 mm (3.4 in) across the range and, naturally, the lenses all feature Cooke’s latest /i Technology for real-time readout of focus and iris position, as well as motion inertial data.

Pricing and availability

The S4 FF/i lenses are priced at £11,000 / €13,000 / $15,000 per lens and are available to order now.
